dataset.what_one_row_represents: Varies by file: regime-month-category aggregate (mobility table); country-day (Google Mobility, OxCGRT); country-year (BMR democracy, Polity, Maddison); single epidemic event (EM-DAT); country snapshot (Freedom House)
dataset.time_range: March–May 2020 for COVID-era files; 1800–2016 for regime classifications; 1963–2020 for EM-DAT epidemics

ana_01.label: April 2020 mobility gap, by category
ana_01.content: In April 2020 — the global lockdown peak — democracies dropped mobility further than non-democracies in every Google category. The gap was largest at workplaces (-59.0% vs -44.3%, a 14.7-point difference) and at retail and recreation (-75.6% vs -61.9%, 13.7 pp). Even at parks (-51.9% vs -38.5%, 13.4 pp) and grocery and pharmacy (-46.2% vs -38.1%, 8.1 pp) the picture is the same. The smallest gap is at transit stations (-67.2% vs -63.0%, 4.2 pp), the one place where authoritarian states posted comparable drops, plausibly because public-transport closures are easier to enforce by decree than private behaviour.

ana_02.label: Monthly trajectory: gap is consistent March–May
ana_02.content: Pooling all five mobility categories, democracies kept a 10–13 point larger reduction than non-democracies in every month of the spring 2020 wave: a 13.0-pp gap in March, 10.8-pp in April, and 11.0-pp in May. Both groups eased somewhat from March to May (democracies moved from -61.1% to -50.8%; non-democracies from -48.1% to -39.8%), but the gap did not close. The picture is therefore not a one-week artefact of when each country happened to lock down — it persists across the whole quarter.

ana_03.content: The full chart-ready table for the central visualisation: 30 rows covering every combination of month (March, April, May), category (5 Google mobility categories), and regime (Democracies, Non-Democracies). For each cell we have the mean change from baseline plus the published top-90 / bot-90 percentile band, which is what the Economist used to draw error whiskers.

ana_04.label: Peak gap: April retail & recreation
ana_04.content: The single largest gap in the dataset is April retail and recreation: democracies fell to -75.6% of baseline, non-democracies only to -61.9%, a 13.7-point chasm. Retail and recreation is also the category most clearly tied to voluntary behaviour rather than state coercion — going to a restaurant or a cinema is a discretionary trip — which lines up with the article's argument that compliance, not legal severity, drove the gap.

ana_05.label: May 2020: workplaces become the widest gap
ana_05.content: In May, as countries began to reopen, the gap between democracies and non-democracies actually widened at workplaces (-47.0% vs -31.6%, 15.4 pp) and stayed wide at retail and recreation (-65.8% vs -52.9%, 12.9 pp). Non-democracies returned to their workplaces faster — consistent with formal rules being relaxed centrally — while democratic publics, where the trade-off was more individualised, kept staying home.

ana_06.label: Within-group dispersion is similar across regime types
ana_06.content: Mean dispersion (top-90 minus bot-90 percentile band, averaged across all rows) is 48.7 points for democracies and 49.9 points for non-democracies — essentially identical. The story is therefore not 'democracies are uniformly compliant; autocracies vary wildly'. Both groups contain countries all over the spectrum; what differs is the centre of mass. This is the right caveat to put on any single-country comparison.

data_table.description: Average dispersion (top_90 - bot_90, percentage points) by regime

ana_07.label: Stringency vs mobility: average by regime
ana_07.content: Joining OxCGRT, Google Mobility, and the Boix-Miller-Rosato regime classification at the country level, we get 110 countries with full April 2020 data (74 democracies, 36 non-democracies). The average Stringency Index — what governments asked of citizens — was almost identical across regimes: 79.3 for democracies versus 80.6 for non-democracies. But the average drop in workplace mobility — what citizens actually did — was dramatically larger in democracies: -48.1% versus -38.9%, a 9.2-point gap, despite *lower* nominal stringency. This is the article's central point in one comparison.

ana_08.label: At equal stringency, democracies still moved less
ana_08.content: Holding stringency roughly constant, the gap survives. Among the 62 countries with the strictest April policies (Stringency >= 80), 38 democracies cut workplace mobility to -58.7% while 24 non-democracies only reached -44.9% — a 13.8-point gap at the same level of legal severity. In the medium band (60-80) the gap is 8.4 pp (-40.7 vs -32.3). Only at very low stringency (<60, where there are barely any countries) does the gap vanish. So it isn't that democracies wrote stricter laws; it's that, at any given strictness, their citizens complied more.

ana_09.label: Country-level scatter: stringency vs workplace mobility
ana_09.content: The country-level scatter shows the relationship at full resolution. Democracies cluster in the bottom-right (high stringency, large mobility drop). Notable democracy outliers in the high-compliance corner include Argentina (98.0 stringency, -53.1% mobility), Bolivia (-74.7%), Ecuador (-74.9%), and Spain (-68.6%). Non-democracy outliers in the low-compliance corner include several African states with very high posted stringency but small mobility drops. Japan is a notable democracy outlier in the *other* direction: stringency only 45.7 yet mobility fell 21.9% — voluntary distancing without strict orders.

ana_10.label: Historical EM-DAT: democracies suffered fewer epidemic deaths per outbreak (1960-2020)
ana_10.content: EM-DAT records 1,062 epidemic events from 1960 onwards where regime classification at the start year is available. Democracies experienced 394 of these and lost 68,159 people in total (median 34 deaths per outbreak); non-democracies experienced 668 outbreaks and lost 167,157 people (median 45.5). Median deaths per outbreak were therefore 34% higher in non-democracies. The mean is even more skewed (250.2 vs 173.0) because of catastrophic outliers in non-democracies — although means are dominated by under-reporting issues so the median is the right comparison.

regime                                                              
Democracies            394       68159.0           34.0        173.0
Non-Democracies        668      167157.0           45.5        250.2

data_table.description: Epidemics 1960-2020 in EM-DAT, by regime classification at outbreak year

ana_11.label: Median epidemic deaths by decade and regime
ana_11.content: Decadal medians show the gap is not constant. In the 1960s and 1970s the medians were close. The 1980s look like an anomaly: democracies' median jumped to 183 deaths per outbreak (well above the 100-death median in non-democracies). From the 1990s onwards the pattern flips and stays flipped — non-democracies have higher medians in every decade through the 2010s (62 vs 51 in the 1990s; 28.5 vs 24 in the 2000s; 43 vs 27 in the 2010s). The post-1990 picture is the one most relevant to the COVID-era argument.

data_table.description: Median deaths per epidemic outbreak, by decade and regime (EM-DAT)

ana_12.label: Countries with most recorded epidemics
ana_12.content: EM-DAT's most epidemic-prone countries since 1960 include Nigeria (55 outbreaks, 24,802 deaths), India (55, 20,874), Uganda (34, 1,661), Tanzania (30, 9,486), and Sudan (28, 7,089). Most of the high-frequency entries are in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and the regime split there is dominated by non-democracies. Burkina Faso (23 outbreaks, 17,101 deaths) and Nigeria are the worst on the death side; India is the most striking democracy in the top tier — many outbreaks but a comparatively low total because the country reports faster and treats more aggressively.

caveats.content: Google Mobility coverage skews toward smartphone-rich, Google-using countries — the non-democracy sample is therefore tilted toward middle-income and wealthier autocracies (e.g. Gulf states, Russia) and away from low-income ones.
Stringency Index measures policy on paper, not enforcement. Two countries with identical scores can implement them very differently.

EM-DAT death counts in non-democracies are likely under-reported, which would bias the historical comparison TOWARD democracies looking worse than they are. The fact that non-democracies still post higher medians is therefore a conservative finding.

Income confound: democracies are on average richer, and richer countries have better health systems. The 14-pp mobility gap is partly mediated by ability-to-stay-home (white-collar share, savings, food delivery infrastructure).
Sample of country-level merged data is 110 — adequate but not comprehensive. Several non-democracies that publish little data (notably China) are absent from the Google Mobility extract.
